title: Murim Style Cartoonish Game Made By Gpt 6 Astra
author: No-Expression861
selftext:
Some of you might’ve seen my Dragon Ball arena fighter posts. For that project, I gave Astra existing character models, maps, and effects to work with.  
This time, I wanted to see what it could do without handing it premade game assets.

This is **Under Heaven: Jade Valley**, a chibi martial-arts sect-building game made in Godot. The idea was something inspired by Clash of Clans, but calmer, with farming, fishing, exploration, disciples living around the village, and some tactical combat.

**Astra built the game and created the in-game assets itself. It also handled recording the gameplay and putting this showcase video together.** The footage is an automated playthrough, with sped-up travel and repeated work labeled on screen.

My part was the concept, planning, visual references, and feedback. Reference images aren’t ready-to-use models, so it still had to turn that direction into actual game assets. I’m not claiming I typed “make a game” and came back to a finished product with no input.  
Graphics were my biggest priority. I wanted sculpted chibi characters, layered clothes, nice lighting, moving foliage, water, and a village that actually felt inhabited. Watching it go from one school building to a little settlement with people gathering around it is probably my favorite part.

There’s still stuff I want to improve, especially animation. But seeing it handle the game, assets, and the video itself is honestly wild.

**For people getting into AI game dev, here’s how I’d structure your prompts**

**1. Explain the game you actually want to play.**  
Not just “make a cozy RPG.” Explain what the player does, what they’re working toward, and how the activities connect. In this case, farming and fishing should support life at the school, exploration should bring useful things home, and upgrades should visibly change the village.

**2. Give it references and explain what matters in them.**  
“Make it look AAA” barely communicates anything. I gave it character references and pointed out the proportions, sculpted hair, faces, clothing layers, and finish I wanted. Do the same for environments: explain the lighting, camera angle, building shapes, vegetation, and atmosphere—not just “copy this picture.”

**3. Set an order instead of dumping every feature into one giant request.**  
My brief put the visual foundation first, then a small connected gameplay loop, then the rest of the content. Get one character and one area looking right before asking for a whole roster and map. Otherwise, you risk getting twenty versions of something you already dislike.

**4. Define what “finished” means.**  
A farming system isn’t finished because there’s a button that adds crops to your inventory. The character needs to interact with the plot, the plant needs to grow, harvesting needs to work, and the result needs to persist after saving and loading. Ask it to run the game and inspect the result—not just report that the code has no errors.

**5. Give specific corrections when something is wrong.**  
Animation is a good example. Astra was moving the body part doing the action while leaving everything else stiff. Saying “make the animation better” doesn’t explain the problem. Saying “the arm is doing everything; give the character a supporting stance, weight transfer, torso movement, follow-  
through, and recovery” gives it something concrete to fix.

The basic structure I’d use is:

**What I’m building → what the player does → visual references and priorities → constraints → implementation order → how to test whether it’s actually done.**

I also explicitly told it not to use sub-agents and to leave the project documented so another coding model could take over without rebuilding everything or lowering the quality.

There isn’t a magic paragraph that guarantees everyone the same result. But I’d spend more time making the brief clear and reviewing what the game actually does, rather than repeatedly telling the model to “try harder.”

**You don’t have to personally write every line of code to contribute something important. Deciding what the game should be, spotting what feels wrong, and giving useful direction are still your part.**
